title: Divorce Leads: How Family Law Firms Get Better Leads | CaseAuthority
meta: Divorce leads explained for family law firms: where divorce and custody leads come from, buying vs earning leads, what to ask a lead vendor, intake and conflict checks.
h1: Divorce Leads: How Family Law Firms Get Leads That Turn Into Clients
lead: Every family law firm needs a steady stream of people who are ready to talk about a divorce or custody matter. Some firms buy those leads. Others earn them through Google, reviews and referrals. Many do a bit of both and are not sure which is working. This guide explains where divorce leads come from, how buying leads compares with earning them, what to ask before you pay for leads, why family law intake is different, and how to tell which leads actually become retained clients.
quick_answer: Divorce leads are people who contact your firm, or agree to be contacted, about a divorce, custody, support or other family law matter. You can buy them from lead companies, pay for them through ads, or earn them through your website, Google Business Profile, reviews and referrals. Bought leads start quickly but are often shared with other firms and stop when you stop paying. Earned leads take longer to build but usually come in with more trust and belong only to you. Whatever the source, judge it by how many leads become retained clients, and remember that family law intake needs careful conflict checks and a calm, respectful first conversation.
takeaways: Judge every source by retained clients, not by how many names it sends.
A lead sold to several firms rewards speed over care. Exclusive leads give you room to help.
People who find you in Google or through a referral often arrive ready to listen.
In family law, the other spouse may call too. Run conflict checks before you learn too much.
People going through a divorce are stressed. A calm, kind first call signs more clients.
Paying for leads is regulated. Check your state rules before you sign anything.

sections.answer: They are people who have contacted your firm, or agreed to be contacted, about a divorce, custody, support or other family law matter.
paras: A divorce lead might be a phone call from someone whose spouse just moved out, a web form sent late at night, a chat message asking about custody, or a name and number passed to you by a lead company. Family law firms often use the term family law leads to cover the wider mix: divorce, child custody, child support, alimony, adoption, prenuptial agreements and protective orders.

Family law leads behave differently from many other practice areas. Some people are in a crisis and need help this week. Others are thinking about divorce and are still months away from making a decision. Both are leads, but they need very different handling, and a good lead process recognizes the difference.
Lead generation is simply the work of producing those contacts on a steady basis. The rest of this guide covers the main ways family law firms do that, and how to judge each one fairly.

sections.h2: Where Do Divorce Leads Come From?
sections.answer: Mainly Google search and Maps, paid ads, referrals from past clients and other professionals, legal directories and lead companies.
paras: Most people looking for a divorce lawyer start online. They search for things like divorce lawyer near me, custody attorney in their city, or how to file for divorce in their state. The firms they see in the map results and at the top of the page get the first calls. Our guide to [[a:local-seo-for-divorce-lawyers|local SEO for divorce lawyers]] explains how firms show up there.

Referrals are the other big source. Past clients, therapists and counselors, financial planners, accountants, mediators and other attorneys all send family law matters to firms they trust. These leads often come in warm, because someone the person trusts has already vouched for you.

Paid sources sit alongside these. Google Ads and Local Services Ads put your firm in front of people searching right now. Social media ads can reach people earlier in their decision. And legal directories and lead companies collect inquiries and pass or sell them to firms.

sections.h2: Should Family Law Firms Buy Divorce Leads?
sections.answer: Sometimes. Bought leads can fill a gap or test a new area, but they are often shared and stop the moment you stop paying.
paras: Buying leads has a place. It can help a new firm get its first clients, fill a quiet month, or test demand in a new county before investing in pages and profiles there. Leads arrive quickly, and you do not need search rankings or reviews to start.

The trade offs are real, though. Many lead companies sell the same divorce lead to several firms, so the person may get three or four calls within minutes. Quality varies widely. Some leads turn out to be people who were only curious, people who already hired someone, or people looking for free advice. And the flow ends when you stop paying, so nothing is built for the long term.

The fair test is simple. Track every bought lead through to whether it became a retained client, then compare what you spent with the fees those clients produced. If the numbers hold up month after month, the source may be worth keeping. If they do not, a low price per lead does not make it a good deal.

sections.h2: What to Ask a Lead Company Before You Buy
sections.answer: Ask whether leads are exclusive, where they come from, how consent is collected, what counts as a bad lead, and how easy it is to leave.
paras: Before you pay anyone for divorce or family law leads, get clear answers to a few questions, ideally in writing.
list: Is each lead sent only to my firm, or to other firms too? If shared, how many?
Where do the leads come from, and can I see what the person saw before contacting you?
How do you record that the person agreed to be contacted by a law firm?
Can I choose which counties and case types I receive, such as custody but not adoption?
What happens with wrong numbers, duplicates, people outside my area or people who already have a lawyer?
How fast are leads delivered: live calls, instant forms or batches?
Is there a long contract, a minimum spend or an automatic renewal?

sections.h2: How Do Family Law Firms Earn Their Own Leads?
sections.answer: By showing up in Google and Maps for the right searches, having clear pages for each type of case, earning reviews and building referral relationships.
paras: Earned leads come straight to your firm, and nobody else is selling the same person to your competitors. For most family law firms, that starts with Google.

Your Google Business Profile decides whether you show in the map results. Your website decides whether you show in the regular results, and it works best with one clear page for each main type of matter you handle, such as divorce, contested custody, child support, high asset divorce, military divorce or protective orders, and for each main county you serve. Helpful pages that answer common questions, such as how long a divorce takes in your state or how custody decisions are made, bring in people earlier in their search. Our [[a:divorce-attorney-content-marketing|content marketing for divorce attorneys]] page covers how firms build that out.

Reviews tie it all together. People going through a divorce read reviews closely, looking for signs that a lawyer is kind, responsive and honest. A steady flow of genuine reviews tends to turn more profile views into calls.

Referral relationships with therapists, financial advisers and other attorneys add another stream of high trust leads. These take time to build, but they often become one of a firm's most reliable sources.

sections.h2: Why Family Law Intake Is Different
sections.answer: Family law callers are often upset, the other spouse may call too, and some callers face safety concerns, so intake needs care, conflict checks and a calm tone.
paras: A divorce or custody call is rarely just a business inquiry. The person may be frightened, angry, grieving or exhausted. A rushed or cold first call can lose a client who would have been a great fit, while a calm, kind and clear call often wins them even if another firm called first.

Conflict checks matter more in family law than in most practice areas, because the other spouse may contact you too, sometimes on purpose. Most firms collect the names of both spouses, and sometimes other key parties, at the very start of the call and run a conflict check before hearing the details of the case.

Safety also deserves attention. Some callers are dealing with abuse or threats. Intake staff should know how to handle those calls with care, how to contact the person safely, and when to share emergency resources.

Finally, many family law firms charge for consultations or ask for a retainer early on. Explaining this clearly and kindly on the first call avoids surprises and helps you spend time with people who are ready to move forward.

sections.h2: Why Do So Many Divorce Leads Never Become Clients?
sections.answer: Slow responses, unclear next steps, cold first calls and no follow up for people who are not ready yet.
paras: When a firm says its leads are bad, the problem is often partly inside the firm. A person who fills in a form on Sunday night and hears back on Tuesday has often already booked a consultation somewhere else.

The most common reasons divorce leads slip away are calls that go to voicemail, forms that wait hours or days for a reply, staff who sound rushed or scripted, no clear next step at the end of the call, and no follow up for people who said they were not ready yet.

That last group matters more in family law than in many areas. Someone thinking about divorce may not act for months. A short, respectful follow up plan, such as a helpful guide by email and a check in later, keeps your firm in mind when they are ready, without pressure.

sections.h2: How Do You Know Which Lead Sources Work?
sections.answer: Record where every lead came from, follow it through to whether the person retained you, and compare spend with retained clients and fees for each source.
paras: Cost per lead is easy to see, so it gets a lot of attention. But it can mislead. A cheap lead that never retains you costs more than a pricier lead that does. The better measures are cost per retained client and, over time, fees per source.

To work this out, your intake team needs to record the source of every lead, every time. Ask how the person found you, tag forms and phone numbers by source where possible, and keep the source attached to the matter. Then, for each source, add up what you spent over a set period and divide by the number of retained clients from that source.
With that in place, you can compare a lead company, Google Ads, your map listing and your referral partners fairly, and move budget toward the sources that actually bring you clients.

sections.h2: How Long Does Each Lead Source Take?
sections.answer: Bought leads and ads can start within days. Search and map visibility usually builds over months. Referral networks build over years.
paras: Bought leads and paid ads can start producing inquiries quickly, though ads often need some fine tuning before they settle. Both stop when spending stops.

Search and map visibility usually takes longer. Many firms see early movement within a few months and steadier results after that, depending on how competitive the area is and where the firm starts from. Once built, it keeps working without paying for each lead.
Referral networks take the longest, but they often bring the warmest leads of all. Many family law firms use faster sources to keep consultations booked while slower, longer lasting sources build up.

sections.h2: What Do Bar Rules Say About Buying Family Law Leads?
sections.answer: Rules vary by state, but most limit paying anyone to recommend you and expect lead services not to mislead people. Check your state bar before signing.
paras: Lawyer advertising and paying for leads are regulated, and the rules differ by state. Many states follow some version of the ABA Model Rules, which generally do not allow a lawyer to pay someone for recommending them, while allowing payment for the reasonable cost of advertising and for certain lead generation services.

In general terms, a service that passes along inquiries is treated differently from one that tells people a particular lawyer is the right choice. Lead services are also expected to be honest about who they are and how lawyers are chosen. Some states have their own ethics opinions on lead generation and paying per lead.

Before signing any lead agreement, read how the company presents itself to the public and how it charges you, then check your state bar's rules and ethics opinions. Your firm, not the vendor, is responsible for staying within them.

sections.answer: Timelines and examples here are general. Results vary, and nothing here is legal or ethics advice.
paras: Any timelines or examples in this guide are general and for illustration only. They are not promises of results for your firm. Results from any lead source vary by area, competition, case types, reviews, intake and the work done.

Nothing here is legal, ethics or compliance advice. Rules on lawyer advertising, paying for leads, referral fees, client contact and conflicts of interest vary by state. Check your state bar's rules and speak with your own advisers before buying leads or changing your marketing.

faq.a: Divorce leads are people who have contacted a family law firm, or agreed to be contacted, about a divorce, custody, support or other family law matter. They can be bought, paid for through ads, or earned through search, reviews and referrals.

faq.q: Are Exclusive Divorce Leads Worth More Than Shared Leads?
faq.a: Usually, yes. An exclusive lead goes only to your firm, so you can take time to help the person properly. A shared lead goes to several firms at once, which turns the first call into a race.

faq.q: Where Do Family Law Firms Get the Best Leads?
faq.a: For many family law firms, Google search and Maps, referrals from past clients and other professionals, and strong reviews produce the most trusting leads. The right mix depends on your area and the cases you want, and is best judged by retained clients per source.

faq.q: Why Should Family Law Intake Run a Conflict Check First?
faq.a: Because the other spouse or another party to the matter may also contact your firm. Collecting key names and running a conflict check before hearing the details helps protect both the caller and your firm.

faq.q: How Fast Should a Family Law Firm Respond to a New Lead?
faq.a: As quickly as you can, ideally within minutes. People going through a divorce often contact more than one firm, and a prompt, kind response gives you a real advantage.

faq.q: Is It Legal for Lawyers to Buy Divorce Leads?
faq.a: In many states lawyers can pay for advertising and certain lead services, but there are limits, especially on paying someone to recommend a particular lawyer. Rules vary by state, so check your state bar before signing any lead agreement.
